identity.notes: Community clients configure units by a fixed MAC address inside Weber's IEEE block (70:91:8F), so the address is public and stable. The vendor app shows the model display name plus the address's last four hex digits (for example iGrill2-XXXX). A client wanting the same label can build it that way.

methods.notes: Name OR service UUID. The regex is the app's own case-insensitive prefix test (it lowercases the name first), spelled with character classes so it compiles the same everywhere. It covers the iGrill models ("igrill_...") and the Pulse grills ("pulse 1000" / "pulse 2000"). The Kitchen Thermometers are left to their service UUIDs. A unit that is already connected to a phone usually stops advertising (see device.pairing.exclusivity).

host_compatibility.basis: The vendor app's own connection code carries handset-specific bonding workarounds (older LG, Motorola, Nexus and Samsung devices), removes and remakes the bond when the handshake fails, and retries on GATT status 129. Store reviews from 2019-2024 report Samsung phones that never pair. The vendor manuals give an Android-only fix: unpair in Bluetooth settings, restart Bluetooth from the app, reset the device.
host_compatibility.notes: The vendor app is an Android client, so the stack can drive the device, but only after its bond handling is coaxed along. The workaround is host-side: clear the OS bond (and, per the manuals, reset the device) and pair again.

host_compatibility.basis: The Weber iGrill app ships for iPhone and iPad, and the vendor manuals give iOS pairing instructions (accept the pairing request; forget the device under the blue (i) to recover).

The Linux community clients (bendikwa/igrill, kins-dev/igrill-smoker) use bluepy, which opens the ATT channel itself instead of going through bluetoothd's GATT client. They tell users to create the bond with bluetoothctl first and document a "stuck on Authenticating" failure fixed by Bluetooth adapter settings. Nobody reports driving the device through bluetoothd's own GATT client.

mac_prefixes.notes: IEEE assigns this block to Weber-Stephen Products LLC, and bendikwa/esphome-igrill's discovery helper finds iGrill units by exactly this prefix. It covers everything Weber ships with a radio, though, including the Wi-Fi Weber Connect products, so treat it as supporting evidence beside a name or service match. Units built in the iDevices era may carry iDevices' own block (D4:81:CA), but no source shows one, so that prefix is not listed.

identification.notes: The vendor app identifies a model from the advertised local name alone. It lowercases the name and matches a model prefix (see protocol_details.model_identification). Community clients match the per-model service UUID instead: 1mckenna/esp32_iGrill matches it in the advertisement for the mini, mini v2, iGrill 2, iGrill 2 v2.02 and iGrill 3, and bendikwa/esphome-igrill after connecting. Whether the Kitchen Thermometers and Pulse grills advertise their service UUID is not established. The only advertised name recorded verbatim in a source is "iGrill_mini" (esphome-igrill's discovery log). The "iGrill_" prefix here is that spelling generalised, and a name that does not match it may still be one of these devices. The Kitchen Thermometers match the very short app prefix "kt", which is too generic to use as a matcher, so they are found by service UUID only.

device.name: Weber iGrill Bluetooth Thermometers (iGrill mini, mini v2, iGrill 2, iGrill 3, Kitchen Thermometer, Pulse 1000/2000 probes)
device.notes:
A family of BLE cooking thermometers that iDevices designed and Weber sold after buying iDevices' grilling line. One Android/iOS app, Weber iGrill (package com.weber.igrill), drives all of them. The app's model table gives the probe counts: iGrill mini (1), iGrill mini v2 (1), iGrill 2 and its v2.2 revision (4), iGrill 3 (4, mounted on a Genesis II gas grill, with a propane tank gauge), Kitchen Thermometer (2), Kitchen Thermometer Mini (1), and the thermometer built into the Pulse 1000 (2) and Pulse 2000 (4) electric grills.
VENDOR STATUS. The sources disagree. Our research notes call the line discontinued, and Weber's own 2024 UK PSTI statement lists the end of security updates for the iGrill Mini and iGrill 2 as 1 Jan 2021 and for the iGrill 3, Pulse 1000 and Pulse 2000 as 2021 too. But the app was still being updated (Play listing: version 5.8.1, updated 2025-10-16), and the original iGrill Classic has already been dropped from it. Hence `unsupported`: the hardware is out of vendor support and depends on an app that is still published.
TRANSPORT. BLE GATT, fully local. The phone bonds with the thermometer (Just Works, no passkey), then runs an application-layer challenge-response on service 64ac0000-4a4b-4b58-9f37-94d3c52ffdf7 (see `initialization` and protocol_details.authentication). After that it reads and subscribes to the probe characteristics. The vendor's Firebase account cloud only syncs accounts, recipes and session history. Nothing on the thermometer path goes through it.
CHARACTERISTICS, NOT SERVICES. The temperature surface is one set of characteristics on the base 06efxxxx-2e06-4b79-9e33-fce2c42805ec (config 0001, probe temperatures 0002/0004/0006/0008, per-probe alarms 0003/0005/0007/0009, ambient 000a, ambient alarm 000b). Each model serves that same set under its own model-specific primary service UUID (see `variants` and `services`). The vendor app finds every characteristic by its characteristic UUID alone and never names a service, so a client can do the same. The model service is still the best way to tell models apart.
TEMPERATURES. A probe value is a signed int16, little-endian, in WHOLE degrees. The unit is flagged in the same notification (byte 2, bit 7: 0 = F, 1 = C) and follows the unit set in the config characteristic. Any value below -500 means no probe is plugged in, and the device sends -2000 (raw 30 f8) for that. Alarm thresholds are int16 LE pairs (low, then high) in whole degrees of the configured unit, and -2000 disables either side. The thresholds live on the device: the manuals describe the unit's own LED and tone reacting to the target, and the app writes them to the device.
CORRECTIONS TO EARLIER NOTES. Our screenshot summary claimed "no encryption" and "0.1 degree units". Both are wrong: the app runs an AES handshake and parses whole degrees. The names shown on the vendor screenshots (iGrill2-XXXX, iGrill Mini-XXXX, iGrill²-XXXX) are the app's DISPLAY names, built from the model's display name plus the last two octets of the MAC address. They are not advertised names. See protocol_details.model_identification for what the device advertises.
OUT OF SCOPE. The Pulse grills' heater and controller service (6c910000-58dc-41c7-943f-518b278ceaaa). It heats, so it is safety-sensitive, and nothing here documents controlling it. Also out of scope: OTA payloads and flashing byte sequences (the update mechanism is described by role only, in features and protocol_details.firmware_update), the original iGrill Classic (dropped from the app), the Wi-Fi Weber Connect / SmokeFire products, and the Firebase account cloud.
KEYS. The handshake's keyed form uses a per-model-family 16-byte AES key held in the vendor app. Those keys are deliberately NOT published here. A client does not need one, because the key-free form of the handshake that every current community client uses works without it (see protocol_details.authentication).

openness.notes: Weber never published this protocol. Everything here comes from the vendor app's static analysis, from community clients that have run against the hardware, and from the owner's manuals.

enter_pairing_mode.indicator: The Bluetooth LED, or the Smart LED ring on the mini models, blinks blue while the unit is discoverable and awaiting pairing, and turns solid blue once paired (vendor manuals).

exclusivity.notes: single_connection comes from esphome-igrill's README (units cannot keep multiple connections, and the app cannot be open at the same time) and from the Pulse manual (a solid Bluetooth light means it is already paired to a phone). The manuals cover pairing several iGrills to one phone, never one iGrill to several phones, so whether a unit keeps more than one bond is unknown.
exclusivity.recovery: Close the vendor app and turn Bluetooth off on any other phone that used the thermometer, then connect. If pairing still fails, forget the device in the phone's Bluetooth settings and press the device's reset (device.setup.factory_reset).

pairing.notes: Link layer: an unauthenticated (Just Works) bond with encryption. The manuals show the phone's own pairing request, and the vendor app bonds through the OS before it connects. The community clients all turn on link encryption without MITM protection before reading anything (esp32_iGrill bonds with IO capability "none", esphome-igrill requests encryption, and bendikwa/igrill uses bluepy's "medium" security level). 1mckenna/esp32_iGrill's comment is that without bonding you cannot read the probe temperatures, and bendikwa/igrill tells users to bond with bluetoothctl first. The real authorisation sits above the link, in the AES challenge-response in top-level `initialization`, which runs on every connection whether or not a bond exists. Confidence is medium because the bond requirement comes from open implementations and manuals, not from our own hardware.

unpair.notes: No bond-only clear is documented. The manuals' route is to forget the device on the phone and press the device's reset (device.setup.factory_reset). Nobody has established whether that reset clears anything besides the bond.

issued_to_client: The BLE bond on the client side. No application-layer credential is issued; the handshake key is a per-model constant, and the key-free form of the handshake needs none.
credentials.notes: No Wi-Fi and no account on the device path. The handshake's AES key is a per-model-family constant held in the vendor app, not a per-unit secret, and it is not published here (see protocol_details.authentication).
stored_on_device: BLE bonding keys for each phone that paired (Just Works).

factory_reset.description: Every procedure below comes from the vendor manuals' pairing troubleshooting sections, which always pair it with "forget or unpair the device in the phone's Bluetooth settings first". No reset is documented for the Pulse grills. Their manual only says to turn off Bluetooth on the phone that holds the connection.
factory_reset.effect: Clears the thermometer's stored Bluetooth pairing so a phone can pair again. The manuals present it only as the fix for a failed pairing. Whether it also clears the temperature unit and the stored alarm thresholds is not documented.

procedures.basis: Weber iGrill Mini user manual (2016) and iDevices Kitchen Thermometer mini user manual, pairing troubleshooting sections.
procedures.indicator: The Smart LED light ring turns solid white (the manuals' 'powering off or reset complete').
procedures.name: Reset pin under the battery door, 5 s (mini-format units)

steps.action: Forget or unpair the thermometer in the phone's Bluetooth settings, and turn the phone's Bluetooth off.
Lift the thermometer off its magnetic base. With it still powered on, remove the battery door.
Press the recessed reset button with a pin for about 5 seconds, until the light ring turns white, then refit the battery door.

procedures.basis: Weber iGrill 2 user manual (2016) and iDevices Kitchen Thermometer user manual, pairing troubleshooting sections.
procedures.indicator: The display's power-on animation runs (the manuals: it animates during power-on and during reset).
procedures.name: Reset pin under the battery door, 5 s (display units)

steps.action: Forget or unpair the thermometer in the phone's Bluetooth settings, and turn the phone's Bluetooth off.
With the unit powered on, remove the battery door and press the reset button with a pin (or a probe tip) for five seconds, then refit the door.

procedures.basis: Weber iGrill 3 user manual (2016), pairing troubleshooting section.
procedures.name: Hold the power button 15 s (iGrill 3)

steps.action: Forget or unpair the iGrill 3 in the phone's Bluetooth settings, and turn the phone's Bluetooth off.
With the iGrill 3 powered on, press and hold the power button on its faceplate for 15 seconds.

methods.description: Power the thermometer on, connect, encrypt the link with a Just Works bond, write 16 zero bytes to 64ac0002, read 16 bytes from 64ac0003, and write those same 16 bytes back to 64ac0004. Then read the unit from 06ef0001 and subscribe to the probe characteristics.
methods.name: Bond, then run the key-free challenge handshake

steps.action: Power the thermometer on (a short press of the power button on the mini, iGrill 2 and Kitchen Thermometers; the iGrill 3 and Pulse controller power on with their grill). Close the vendor app, and turn Bluetooth off on any phone that last used it.
steps.expect: The Bluetooth LED (the Smart LED ring on the mini models) blinks blue: discoverable and waiting to pair. A solid blue light on a Pulse means it is already paired and connected to another phone.

steps.action: Scan for a per-model service UUID or a matching name (device.discovery), then connect.
Raise link security to encrypted and bond (Just Works, no MITM, no passkey). On a phone the OS shows a pairing request.
Accept the operating system's Bluetooth pairing request, if the host shows one.

Run the handshake in top-level `initialization`: write 16 x 0x00 to 64ac0002-4a4b-4b58-9f37-94d3c52ffdf7, read 16 bytes from 64ac0003-4a4b-4b58-9f37-94d3c52ffdf7, and write those bytes unchanged to 64ac0004-4a4b-4b58-9f37-94d3c52ffdf7.
Read 06ef0001-2e06-4b79-9e33-fce2c42805ec. Byte 0 is the temperature unit every reading and threshold is in (0 = F, 1 = C).

Subscribe to probe 1 (06ef0002-2e06-4b79-9e33-fce2c42805ec) and, on models that have them, probes 2-4 (06ef0004, 06ef0006, 06ef0008 on the same base) and ambient (06ef000a). Also subscribe to battery 00002a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and, on the iGrill 3, propane f5d40001-3548-4c22-9947-f3673fce3cd9.
steps.expect: Notifications carrying int16 LE whole degrees with the unit in byte 2 bit 7. -2000 means no probe.

timing.bond_basis: The vendor app starts an OS bond before connecting, polls the bond state every 500 ms, and gives up after 30 s.
timing.handshake_timeout_basis: The vendor app abandons the 64ac0002 write, 64ac0003 read and 64ac0004 write sequence after 30 s.
timing.inter_step_delay_basis: esp32_iGrill leaves 500 ms to 1 s between the handshake steps. The vendor app does not wait. Both are reported to work.

causes: The link is not encrypted. The community clients all force encryption or bonding before reading (esp32_iGrill: without bonding you cannot read the probes). Bond first, then run the handshake.
The handshake was not run on this connection. It is per connection, not per bond.
troubleshooting.symptom: The handshake completes but reads of the probe characteristics fail, or never return.

causes: Another phone or the vendor app holds the one connection. esphome-igrill's README says the units cannot keep more than one connection. Close the vendor app and turn Bluetooth off on the other phone (the Pulse manual gives the same advice).
The unit has powered itself off. Unpaired, the mini, iGrill 2 and iGrill 3 turn off after 5 minutes with no probe and after 8 hours with a probe fitted (vendor manuals).
troubleshooting.symptom: The device is not found, or connecting times out.

causes: A stale bond on one side. The manuals' fix: unpair the device in the phone's Bluetooth settings, restart Bluetooth, then press the device's reset (setup.factory_reset) and pair again.

The vendor app itself removes the bond and bonds again when the handshake fails, and treats GATT status 129 (0x81) as retryable. A replacement client should do the same rather than give up on the first error.

The vendor app carries phone-specific bonding workarounds (older LG, Motorola and Nexus handsets, and Samsung devices), and store reviews report Samsung phones that never pair. See device.host_compatibility.
troubleshooting.symptom: Pairing keeps failing on Android, or the phone lists the device as paired but the app cannot use it.

causes: A vendor-app defect, not a device requirement as far as anyone has shown. A replacement client should reconnect with the existing bond and rerun the handshake. Only if the device refuses should it clear the bond on both sides.
troubleshooting.symptom: After leaving Bluetooth range, the vendor app never reconnects until the unit is reset and paired again (repeated store reviews, 2020-2024).

causes: The unit was assumed rather than read. Every reading and threshold is in the unit set in 06ef0001 byte 0, and each probe notification repeats it in byte 2 bit 7. The vendor app converts and rewrites every probe's thresholds when the unit changes, and the device does not do this itself.
troubleshooting.symptom: Temperatures look wrong by the Fahrenheit/Celsius ratio, or thresholds fire at the wrong point.

causes: No probe is plugged in. The value is the int16 -2000 (raw 30 f8), and 63536 is that same value read as unsigned. bendikwa/igrill reads the field as unsigned, so negative temperatures also come out wrong there.

setup.notes: Nothing is provisioned: there is no Wi-Fi, no account and no credential to hand over. Every connection needs two things, a Just Works bond at the link layer (device.pairing) and the challenge handshake on 64ac0002 .. 64ac0004 (top-level initialization). The vendor app does both automatically, and the manuals only tell the user to accept the phone's pairing request. Confidence is medium. Two working open implementations (esphome-igrill, esp32_iGrill) run exactly this flow on hardware across most of the family, but this project has not replayed it.

rejoin.notes: There is no network to rejoin. To move a unit to a new phone or client, disconnect the old one (close its app, turn its Bluetooth off) and pair from the new one. The Pulse manual says that is enough. If the unit then refuses the new bond, forget it on the old phone and run the reset in factory_reset.

testing.notes: Nobody on this project has driven one of these thermometers from this document, and our research store holds no capture of one. The byte layouts come from static analysis of the vendor app (Weber iGrill 5.8.1) and are cross-checked against community clients. Those clients report hardware success: bendikwa/esphome-igrill lists the iGrill mini, iGrill 2, iGrill 2 v2.02, iGrill 3, Pulse 1000, Pulse 2000 and iDevices Kitchen Thermometer as confirmed working, and 1mckenna/esp32_iGrill credits testers for the mini, mini v2, v2.02 and iGrill 3. That is `reported` evidence for us, not `confirmed`.

variants.notes: One probe, CR2032 coin cell, Smart LED ring. esphome-igrill and esp32_iGrill both detect it by this service (esphome-igrill lists it as confirmed). The app's name prefix is "igrill_mini". Reset: the pin under the battery door (setup.factory_reset).

One probe. esp32_iGrill calls this the newer mini model and credits a hardware tester for it. The vendor app matches it by the name prefix "igrill_mini02" (checked before "igrill_mini") or "igrill_mini_2". The app's model table attaches this service UUID to its plain "iGrill mini" entry instead (see protocol_details.model_identification).
Four probes, 2x AA, display with probe toggle buttons. Confirmed working in esphome-igrill. App name prefix "igrill_v2". The vendor app carries no constant for this service UUID.

Four probes. The community calls it iGrill v202 (esphome-igrill lists it as confirmed, and esp32_iGrill calls it the newer iGrill 2 model). The vendor app has a separate "iGrill 2 v2.2" model (name prefix "igrill_v2_2") but attaches this service UUID to its plain "iGrill 2" entry. Which advertised name this revision carries is not recorded.

Four probes. Mounted on Genesis II / LX gas grills, 3x AA battery pack. Adds the propane tank gauge (service f5d40000-3548-4c22-9947-f3673fce3cd9) and, wired to a Genesis II LX, the grill's lit control knobs (protocol_details.knob_lights). App name prefix "igrill_v3". Reset: hold the power button 15 s.
Two probes, 2x AA. Originally the iDevices Kitchen Thermometer (iDevices Connected app). esphome-igrill lists it as confirmed by this service. App name prefix "kt".
One probe, coin cell. The service UUID comes only from the vendor app's model table, and no community client has seen it on hardware. App name prefix "kt_mini".

Electric grill with a built-in iGrill: two probes plus the grill's own controller. Only the thermometer surface is covered here. esphome-igrill lists the thermometer service as confirmed. App name prefix "pulse 1000". Mains powered, so no battery characteristic is expected. When the unit changes, the app also writes the controller's own one-byte unit setting, with the opposite encoding (protocol_details.pulse_controller_service).
Electric grill with a built-in iGrill and four probes; otherwise as the Pulse 1000. esphome-igrill lists it as confirmed. App name prefix "pulse 2000".

entities.name: Probe 1 Temperature
entities.notes: Whole degrees in the unit the device is set to (unit_flag in the same notification, or 06ef0001 byte 0). Show "no probe" for any value below -500 rather than rendering -2000.

entities.name: Ambient Temperature
entities.notes: Unscoped because nobody knows which models serve 06ef000a. Create it only when the characteristic exists on the connected unit.

entities.name: Probe 1 Target
entities.notes: The high alarm, which is the app's "peak" target. Setting it writes low = -2000 (disabled). -2000 read back means no target is set. It is in the device's unit: -22 to 572 F or -30 to 300 C, per the manuals' display range.

entities.name: Temperature Unit
entities.notes: After changing the unit, convert each probe's stored thresholds and rewrite them, as the vendor app does. The device keeps the old numbers otherwise. On a Pulse the app also sets the grill controller's own display unit (protocol_details.pulse_controller_service).

entities.name: Propane Level
entities.notes: Quarter-tank steps. Treat sensor_fault, or a raw step above 4, as unavailable.

evidence.app_static_analysis: Weber iGrill 5.8.1 for Android, decompiled. The app is obfuscated, but its BLE log strings name every characteristic role. It established: the model table (nine models, probe counts, name prefixes, service UUID constants), the bond-then-connect-then-authenticate flow and its 30 s timeouts, the handshake's arithmetic and its AES/ECB/NoPadding cipher setup, the probe parser (int16 LE, whole degrees, byte 2 bit 7 unit, below -500 absent), the alarm pair layout and the -2000 sentinel, the configuration block's unit and acknowledgement bytes and the app's read-modify-write of it, the ambient alarm on 06ef000b, the propane parser and fault bit, the knob-light characteristics, the Pulse controller characteristics' roles, the three update paths (role only), and the display-name rule. Nothing from it is reproduced beyond UUIDs and byte layouts. The per-model keys it contains are deliberately left out.

artifacts.description: The vendor app. Source of every byte layout marked reported here. Its embedded model keys are not reproduced.

ESPHome component: per-model service UUIDs, key-free handshake after forcing encryption, threshold read/write verified against an HCI capture on an iGrill 2, propane, Pulse element read, and the confirmed-model list.

Arduino ESP32 client: advertised service matching, just-works bonding setup, key-free handshake, single-byte unit write, propane, and credits for hardware testers on the mini, mini v2, v202 and iGrill 3.
Python/bluepy MQTT bridge, deprecated in favour of esphome-igrill. Key-free handshake since release 2.0, and bonding advice.
Where the key-free handshake is explained. Signed int16 reads and two-int16 threshold writes.
The original keyed client. It checks the decrypted first half of the device challenge against its own challenge, which is where the plaintext layout comes from.

evidence.capture_review: None. Our research store holds no capture of any model in this family.
evidence.documentation_review: Weber-hosted manuals: iGrill Mini (2016), iGrill 2 (2016), iGrill 3 (2016), Pulse 2000 (US 2022) and Pulse 1000/2000 (GB 2018). The iDevices Kitchen Thermometer and Kitchen Thermometer mini manuals, via the Internet Archive. Weber's 2024 UK PSTI statement for iGrill products. They gave the pairing indicators, reset procedures, auto-shut-off timings, peak and range alarm behaviour, fuel gauge and knob lights, and the security support end dates. No manual prints an FCC ID.
evidence.open_questions: See remaining_unknowns. What to settle first with a unit in hand: the exact advertised names per model, whether a 1-byte write to 06ef0001 keeps bytes 1-4, and one HCI capture of the vendor app's keyed handshake and an alarm acknowledgement.
evidence.open_source_review: kvantetore/igrill (the original keyed client; confirms the device plaintext layout). kins-dev/igrill-smoker @ 5dc78b5f (the key-free handshake, signed reads, threshold writes as two int16 LE). bendikwa/igrill @ e42dba40 (key-free handshake, bonding advice). bendikwa/esphome-igrill @ b5edba3c (model detection by service UUID, encryption before authentication, threshold read and write, propane, Pulse element read, hardware-confirmed model list). 1mckenna/esp32_iGrill @ 45c5f1d3 (advertised-service matching, just-works bond parameters, single-byte unit write, propane, credited hardware testers).

dfu_mode.notes: How a unit advertises mid-update is not established.

enter.notes: The vendor app writes an update-begin command to 64ac0005-4a4b-4b58-9f37-94d3c52ffdf7 and then streams on the same connection. Whether the radio reboots into a loader in between is not established. The command's bytes are deliberately withheld (brick risk), so no entry command is declared.

image.format: Intel HEX for the BLE radio module (8051-core addressing, consistent with a TI CC254x-class SoC). The Pulse grills' controller takes raw ARM Cortex-M (STM32-class) binaries.
image.notes: The app fetches images from a vendor object store. One Pulse controller image also ships inside the app. No image, file name, digest or byte is reproduced here, and whether the bootloader checks a signature is unknown.

dfu.notes: Role-level only. The vendor app has three update paths. (1) A block stream: the update-begin command on 64ac0005, then image blocks written to 00060001-f8ce-11e4-abf4-0002a5d5c51b, whose notifications pace the transfer. (2) An Intel-HEX record stream written to 64ac0005 itself, rebased by a per-model address offset. (3) On the Pulse grills, fixed-size checksummed packets to the controller service's update characteristic, with status notifications back. The service that holds 00060001 is not recorded. See protocol_details.firmware_update.

initialization.notes: App challenge, key-free form: 16 zero bytes (kins-dev/igrill-smoker, bendikwa/igrill, esphome-igrill, esp32_iGrill). The vendor app writes 8 random bytes followed by 8 zero bytes instead, and then needs the model's AES key (protocol_details.authentication). Run this only on an encrypted (bonded) link. Write with response.
The device's challenge: 16 bytes, AES-128-ECB-encrypted under the model key. With the zero challenge above, its plaintext begins with eight zero bytes, which is what makes the next step key-free.

initialization.description: Write the 16 bytes just read from 64ac0003-4a4b-4b58-9f37-94d3c52ffdf7 back to this characteristic, unchanged, with response. No fixed bytes can be stated because the value is fresh on every connection, so a client implements this step itself.
initialization.notes: With the vendor app's random challenge the response is instead AES-128-ECB-encrypt(key, 00 x 8 || bytes 8-15 of AES-128-ECB-decrypt(key, challenge)). See protocol_details.authentication.test_vectors. The vendor app gives the three steps 30 s in total.

The 5-byte configuration block. Byte 0 is the temperature unit that every probe reading and alarm threshold is in (0 = F, 1 = C). The vendor app then writes the block back with byte 2 (the alarm acknowledgement) set to 0. That write is not known to be required, so it is described in protocol_details.configuration rather than run here.

Probe 1, which every model has. Subscribe to probes 2-4 (06ef0004, 06ef0006, 06ef0008), ambient (06ef000a), battery (00002a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb) and propane (f5d40001-3548-4c22-9947-f3673fce3cd9) only where the model serves them. The vendor app attempts all of them and skips any characteristic it cannot find.

alarm_semantics.peak: High side set, low side -2000. The manuals: sounds when the probe reaches the target. On the mini models the LED goes green, then yellow at 15 F (9 C) away, orange at 5 F (3 C) away, blinking red at the target, and solid red once acknowledged.
alarm_semantics.range: Both sides set. Sounds when the probe leaves the band. The app uses it for grill or ambient temperature.
alarm_semantics.unit: Whole degrees in the configured unit. The device does not convert stored thresholds when the unit changes.

authentication.key_free_variant: Write 16 zero bytes as the challenge. Then p[0:8] is already zero, so step 4's plaintext equals step 3's and the response is c itself: read 64ac0003 and write the same 16 bytes to 64ac0004. No key is needed. kins-dev/igrill-smoker worked this out, and bendikwa/igrill (release 2.0, which dropped its crypto dependency), esphome-igrill and esp32_iGrill all use it on hardware across the family. The missing-devices survey asks for the keyed handshake to be confirmed on hardware as well, not only this shortcut. See remaining_unknowns.
authentication.key_handling: K is a 16-byte constant per model family: the vendor app holds six distinct keys for its nine models. They are not reproduced here, in the docs or in any test. A replacement client does not need one. An owner who wants the keyed form can find how the community's first client obtained keys in kvantetore/igrill. The key is a shared product secret, not a per-unit credential, and publishing it would add nothing the key-free form does not already give.
keyed_algorithm: 1. app_challenge = 8 random bytes || 8 zero bytes. Write it to 64ac0002.

2. c = read 64ac0003 (16 bytes). The device computes it as AES-128-ECB-encrypt(K, app_challenge[0:8] || device_nonce[0:8]). The layout is from kvantetore/igrill, which checks the first half. The vendor app does not check it.
4. response = AES-128-ECB-encrypt(K, 8 zero bytes || p[8:16]). Write it to 64ac0004.
5. The vendor app allows 30 s for steps 1-4. On failure it removes the OS bond, reconnects and bonds again.
authentication.summary: A per-connection challenge-response on service 64ac0000-4a4b-4b58-9f37-94d3c52ffdf7, run after the link is encrypted. AES-128 in ECB mode with no padding, over single 16-byte blocks. The mode and padding are written into the vendor app's cipher setup, so this is not a guess from the code's shape. It has still not been captured on the air, so it stays `reported`.

test_vectors.check: openssl enc -aes-128-ecb -nopad -K 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f reproduces each device_challenge_hex from device_plaintext_hex. The response for a given nonce is the same in both vectors, and in the key-free vector it equals the challenge.
test_vectors.key_note: ILLUSTRATIVE KEY ONLY: 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f is the FIPS-197 example key, not a device key. These vectors check an implementation of the arithmetic above, not interoperability with a real unit.

app_behaviour: On connect: read the block, take the unit from byte 0, then write the block back with byte 2 = 0 (the app logs this as resetting the acknowledgement).
When the user dismisses an alarm on the app's alarm screen, the app writes the stored block back with byte 2 = 1.

When the user changes the unit, the app writes the stored block back with byte 0 = the new unit. It then converts each probe's high and low thresholds (F = C x 9/5 + 32 and back, skipping -2000) and rewrites every alarm characteristic.
configuration.layout: 06ef0001: byte 0 unit (0 = F, 1 = C); byte 1 unknown; byte 2 alarm acknowledged (0/1); bytes 3-4 unknown.
configuration.note: Acknowledging an alarm is a read-modify-write of bytes the spec cannot name (1, 3 and 4), so it is not declared as a command. A client that wants it should read 06ef0001, set byte 2 to 1 and write all 5 bytes back.

firmware_update.summary: Role level only, by design. The app fetches images from a vendor object store: Intel HEX for the BLE radio module, and raw Cortex-M binaries for the Pulse controller. It then delivers them over BLE on one of three paths (features[firmware_update].dfu.notes). No update-begin payload, block or record layout, address offset, image name or digest is published, because a wrong one can leave a thermometer unusable and the vendor's images are not ours to redistribute.

characteristics.eaef0001-3909-454c-9d7e-e68cba24a9b8: The app writes the single byte 0x01 when the user taps the light switch in its device settings, which it shows only for the iGrill 3. It is always 0x01, so it behaves like a button press or toggle. It is not written on connect, although earlier notes said so.
characteristics.eaef0002-3909-454c-9d7e-e68cba24a9b8: Read on connect. One byte that the app logs as the LED knob light configuration. Values not established.

knob_lights.not_declared_because: The containing service UUID is not recorded (the app addresses both characteristics by characteristic UUID alone), so no service entry, command or entity is declared for them.
knob_lights.scope: iGrill 3 wired to a Genesis II LX grill's control-knob lights (iGrill 3 manual: the app turns the knob lights on and off, as does the grill's own button).

advertised_name_prefixes.notes: The vendor app lowercases the advertised local name and tests these prefixes, longest first. The mini v2's "igrill_mini02" is special- cased ahead of the list because "igrill_mini" would otherwise swallow it. A name that matches none is not offered to the user. These are the on-air name prefixes the app accepts. The exact casing and suffix a unit sends is on record only for "iGrill_mini".

model_identification.display_name: The app labels a unit with the model's display name, a hyphen, and the last two octets of its MAC without the colon: iGrill Mini-XXXX, iGrill²-XXXX. The vendor screenshots show these labels, and they were earlier mistaken for advertised names.

service_uuid_mapping.notes: Two sources, and they disagree for the mini and the iGrill 2. The community mapping comes from clients that detect the model by these services on hardware. The app's model table carries UUID constants its own code never reads (it identifies models by name), so where the two disagree the community mapping is used in `variants`. One reading that reconciles them: the app's "mini" and "iGrill 2" entries describe the later hardware revisions (9d610c43..., ada7590f...), and the original iDevices-era revisions (63c70000..., a5c50000...) simply have no constant left in the app.

vendor_app_model_table.6c910000-58dc-41c7-943f-518b278ceaaa: Pulse 1000 and Pulse 2000 (the controller service, not the thermometer service)
vendor_app_model_table.no_constant: iGrill mini v2 and iGrill 2 v2.2 carry no service UUID in the app.

pulse_controller_service.roles_only: Per the vendor app: a notify characteristic whose value the app divides by 100 and shows as a temperature. A one-byte controller display-unit write, with the OPPOSITE encoding to 06ef0001 (0 = C, 1 = F), which the app sends alongside every unit change. A one-byte controller firmware-version read. A buzzer-status notify. The controller firmware-update packet write and its status notify. esphome-igrill additionally reads 6c91000a-58dc-41c7-943f-518b278ceaaa as ASCII three-digit fields for the two heating elements' actual and set temperatures, read-only. No write to this service is described, and none should be attempted from a client built on this spec.
pulse_controller_service.status: OUT OF SCOPE. It heats, so it is safety-sensitive, and no control of it is documented here.

source_conflicts.ambient_alarm_role: 06ef000b was listed as role unknown. The app parses and writes it as the ambient sensor's alarm pair.
source_conflicts.brief_advertised_names: iGrill2-XXXX and similar are app display names built from the MAC, not advertised names (model_identification.display_name).
source_conflicts.config_uuid_in_community_code: bendikwa/igrill and kins-dev/igrill-smoker define a CONFIG constant equal to 06ef0002, probe 1's UUID. They never use it. The configuration characteristic is 06ef0001 (vendor app, esp32_iGrill, esphome-igrill).
source_conflicts.eaef0001_on_connect: Earlier notes said 0x01 is written to eaef0001 on connect. In the app it is a user action on the iGrill 3 only (knob_lights).
source_conflicts.ui_summary_encryption_and_resolution: The screenshot summary said 'no encryption' and '0.1 degree units'. The app's code shows an AES handshake and whole degrees, and every community client divides by nothing. The summary was wrong.
source_conflicts.unsigned_reads: bendikwa/igrill and esphome-igrill read the temperature as unsigned 16-bit, so the no-probe value shows as 63536 and a sub-zero reading wraps. The app and kins-dev/igrill-smoker read it signed.
source_conflicts.vendor_status: Research notes: discontinued. Play listing: updated 2025-10-16. Weber's PSTI statement: security support ended 2021. All three are recorded in device.notes.

remaining_unknowns: The exact advertised local name of every model (casing, separator, any suffix). Only 'iGrill_mini' is on record verbatim. The app matches lowercase prefixes (protocol_details.model_identification).

Which service UUID each hardware revision really carries. The community and the app's dead constants disagree for the mini / mini v2 and the iGrill 2 / v2.2 (protocol_details.model_identification.service_uuid_mapping).
Whether the Kitchen Thermometer Mini's 38e70000-43bf-4afa-8170-e45548b5205b holds the 06ef characteristic set. It comes from the app only.
Whether the Kitchen Thermometers and Pulse grills advertise their model service UUID, or show it only after connecting.

The keyed handshake has never been captured on the air, and neither has the key-free one. The cipher mode (AES-128-ECB, no padding) comes from the app's code, and the device's plaintext layout from kvantetore/igrill.
Whether the device rejects an unencrypted link with an ATT error or just stays silent, and whether it keeps more than one bond.
Whether a 1-byte write to 06ef0001 (esp32_iGrill's unit write) leaves config bytes 1-4 intact, and what bytes 1, 3 and 4 mean.
Whether the device enforces thresholds on its own with no phone connected. The manuals and esphome-igrill say the unit alarms itself, but the ambient alarm and the Pulse have not been seen doing so.
Which models serve the ambient pair 06ef000a/06ef000b, and what 'ambient' measures on each (grill air, or the Pulse cook-box sensor?).
The service UUID holding the knob-light characteristics eaef0001/eaef0002, and the meaning of their values.

The service UUID holding the update data characteristic 00060001-f8ce-11e4-abf4-0002a5d5c51b, whether an update reboots the radio into a loader, how a unit advertises mid-update, and whether images are signed. Intentionally unpublished: the update-begin layout.
Whether the Pulse grills serve the battery service.
The original iGrill Classic (dropped from the app) is not covered, and may speak something else entirely. The research notes describe it as a Bluetooth Classic predecessor.
Whether resetting a unit also clears its unit setting and stored thresholds.
No FCC grant has been found for any model (fccid.co holds none under iDevices 2ABDJ or Weber-Stephen 2AHSR), and no manual prints an FCC ID.

characteristics.name: firmware_version
characteristics.notes: UTF-8 firmware version string. The app trims whitespace and logs it, and esp32_iGrill reads it after the handshake.

characteristics.name: app_challenge
characteristics.notes: 16 bytes, written with response. Key-free clients write 16 zero bytes. The vendor app writes 8 random bytes plus 8 zero bytes. See initialization.

characteristics.name: device_challenge
characteristics.notes: 16 bytes: AES-128-ECB(model key, first 8 bytes of the app challenge || 8-byte device nonce). kvantetore/igrill checks the decrypted first half against its own challenge. The vendor app does not check it.

characteristics.name: device_response
characteristics.notes: 16 bytes, written with response: AES-128-ECB(model key, 8 zero bytes || device nonce). This equals the 64ac0003 value whenever the app challenge was all zeros.

characteristics.name: ota_control
characteristics.notes: Firmware-update control point (features[firmware_update]). The vendor app writes an update-begin command here, and one of its update paths also streams image records here. This spec deliberately gives no bytes for either. A generic client must list it read-only and never write it: a wrong write risks leaving the thermometer unusable.

services.name: Authentication and firmware-update service
services.notes: Common to every model. The service UUID comes from the community clients (esphome-igrill, esp32_iGrill). The vendor app addresses its five characteristics by characteristic UUID only. It also carries the firmware-update control point (64ac0005), which a generic client must never write.

format.notes: Whole degrees. Below -500 = no probe (the device sends -2000, raw 30 f8). unit_flag in byte 2 repeats the unit.

format.name: unit_flag
format.notes: Bit 7 of byte 2: this sample's unit. The vendor app decodes with it.

characteristics.name: ambient_temperature
characteristics.notes: The app's fifth, ambient sensor. Layout as probe 1. Which models serve it is unknown.

clear_ambient_alarm.description: Turn both sides off (-2000, -2000), as the app does when a cook ends.

set_ambient_alarm.description: Write the alarm pair. Give only high_alarm for the app's peak alarm (low stays off), or both for a range alarm.

high_alarm.description: Whole degrees. Manual display range: -22 to 572 F, -30 to 300 C.

low_alarm.description: Whole degrees, or -2000 (the default) for off.

format.name: high_alarm
format.notes: The peak target. -2000 = off or never set.

characteristics.name: ambient_alarm
characteristics.notes: The ambient sensor's alarm pair. Layout as probe 1. Earlier notes called this role unknown.

services.name: Pulse 2000 thermometer service
services.notes: The thermometer service of the Pulse 2000 grill (esphome-igrill, confirmed there). Full four-probe set. The controller service is out of scope.

format.name: propane_level
format.notes: Raw 0-4 in quarter-tank steps. A raw value above 4 is a fault, not a reading.

format.name: sensor_fault
format.notes: When set, the app reports the level as a failure regardless of bytes 0-1.

characteristics.name: propane_level
characteristics.notes: At least 3 bytes. Bytes 0-1 are a uint16 LE step from 0 to 4, which the app maps to 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 %. Any other value, or bit 0 of byte 2 set, is a sensor fault. The community clients read byte 0 times 25 and ignore the fault bit. The app warns when the tank drops below a quarter (manual).

services.name: Propane level service
services.notes: iGrill 3 only. It reads the magnetic fuel-level sensor on an LP tank, and natural-gas grills have none (iGrill 3 manual). The vendor app carries this service UUID with the iGrill 3 model, and esp32_iGrill opens it only on the iGrill 3.

services.name: Battery Service
services.notes: Standard SIG battery service. The vendor app reads and subscribes to the level on every model. The Pulse grills are mains powered, and whether they serve it is not established.

characteristics.name: serial_number
characteristics.notes: Per-unit identifier. Never commit a real value.

services.name: Device Information
services.notes: Standard SIG service. The vendor app reads model number, manufacturer name, hardware revision and serial number on connect, as UTF-8 strings. The serial number is per unit: do not log or publish it.
